note: The Atlas reference library. Every term, player, product, policy and market moment in one searchable place. Financial-metric definitions are ported from glossary.json; figures quoted in entries are drawn from the Atlas data files (timeline.json, financing.json), never invented. Entries are grouped by type and each carries a plain-language definition and, where relevant, a source.

entries.definition: Total sales for the year — the top line, before any costs are taken out.
The bottom-line profit after every cost, plus interest and tax. As a share of revenue it is called net margin.
The share of revenue left after the direct cost of making the product. High margins signal pricing power or cheap production.
Profit as a share of revenue after production plus the cost of running the business (R&D, sales, admin), before interest and tax.
Bottom-line profit as a share of revenue, after everything including tax and one-off items.
Cash left after operating the business and buying equipment — the money genuinely free to reinvest or return to shareholders.
Cash generated by the core business before capital spending.
Profit divided by share count, including shares that stock options could create. The per-share figure most tied to the stock price.
A company-adjusted per-share profit that strips out items like stock compensation and acquisition costs. Higher than GAAP, useful but not standardized.
Revenue from AI and server chips specifically — the segment driving the current buildout.
Intel's Data Center and AI segment — its server and AI-chip business.
Revenue from a chip-manufacturing arm. For Intel, mostly internal transfers, so it overstates the external business.
What the company spent developing new chips and technology. Runs high for designers competing at the leading edge.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization, with some items adjusted out. A rough proxy for cash profitability that ignores capital costs.
AI-specific chip revenue — custom accelerators and networking silicon built for hyperscalers.
For Arm, per-chip fees earned on every chip shipped using its designs. Recurring and high-margin.
Up-front fees companies pay to license a chip-design IP portfolio.
The total market value of all shares: today's share price times shares outstanding. Needs a live price feed.
Share price divided by earnings per share — how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual profit.
The same as P/E, but using analysts' forecast of next year's earnings instead of last year's actual result.
Cumulative count of chips built on a company's designs — a scale indicator for an IP licensor.

How every figure in the Atlas is tagged for confidence: reported (straight from a filing), disclosed (official but via an unofficial channel), estimated (third-party or calculated), or inferred (deduced, not stated). Announced commitments are marked separately from booked figures.
A chip company that designs silicon but outsources the actual manufacturing to a foundry. NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom are fabless — they architect chips that TSMC builds.
A contract chip manufacturer that fabricates other companies' designs. TSMC is the dominant leading-edge foundry, handling the vast majority of advanced AI silicon.
A cloud giant that runs data centers at massive scale — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, Oracle — and is among the largest buyers of AI chips, increasingly designing its own.
A newer cloud provider specialized in renting out GPU compute for AI, rather than general-purpose cloud. CoreWeave is the archetype.
A nation building its own AI compute and models as strategic infrastructure, often through state-backed funds — e.g. Saudi Arabia's HUMAIN and the UAE's G42.

A US framework issued in January 2025 that sorted the world into tiers and capped how many advanced AI chips each could import, to control the global spread of AI compute. It was rescinded on May 13, 2025 — the same day Saudi Arabia's HUMAIN launched.

US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) rules restricting sales of the most advanced AI chips and chipmaking tools to China and elsewhere. First blocked NVIDIA's A100/H100 in October 2022 and have tightened repeatedly since.

The Japanese investment giant led by Masayoshi Son, and a mega-backer of the AI buildout: it committed $41B to OpenAI (for ~11%), anchors the Stargate infrastructure project, and took a $2B stake in Intel.

Through the Commerce Department's BIS, Washington decides who may buy the most advanced AI chips — and has itself become a chip investor, taking a ~10% (~$8.9B) stake in Intel in 2025. Its export policy is a permanent force shaping where demand can legally flow.
State investment funds of the Gulf — chiefly Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) and Abu Dhabi's vehicles — pouring capital into AI compute and sovereign-AI champions like HUMAIN and G42.
An Abu Dhabi state-backed investment vehicle focused on AI and semiconductors; one of the partners in the $500B Stargate infrastructure commitment.
Saudi Arabia's PIF-backed national AI champion, unveiled in May 2025 with NVIDIA to build large-scale (500 MW+) AI data centers — a flagship of sovereign AI.
The UAE's state-linked AI firm, a hub of Gulf sovereign-AI ambitions and a cleared recipient of advanced-chip exports (up to ~70,000 Blackwell GPUs alongside HUMAIN).

Extreme-ultraviolet lithography — the machines that print the finest features on a chip. ASML is the sole maker, and TSMC uses them to fabricate leading-edge AI silicon. The single hardest chokepoint in the whole chain.
NVIDIA's Hopper-generation data-center GPUs — the H100, and the higher-memory H200 — that powered the first wave of the AI boom. Their ramp drove NVIDIA's 2023 demand-signal quarter.
NVIDIA's GPU architecture unveiled in March 2024 (GB200 and successors) — the next-generation accelerators the whole supply chain raced to build, filling the giant new data-center campuses.
NVIDIA's next accelerator platform after Blackwell on its public roadmap, named for the astronomer — signalling the near-annual cadence of ever-more-powerful (and power-hungry) AI chips.

High-bandwidth memory — DRAM stacked in a tower and placed right next to an AI accelerator. Supplied mainly by SK Hynix, with Micron and Samsung. The genuine bottleneck on how many accelerators can ship.
Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate — TSMC's advanced packaging that fuses logic and HBM memory into one finished accelerator. Its limited capacity is a key chokepoint everyone queues for.

On January 27, 2025, a low-cost Chinese model from DeepSeek triggered NVIDIA's ~$600B single-day market-value drop — the largest in market history — and the first serious scare that AI might need far less compute than assumed.

The pattern where a chip vendor invests in — or finances — a customer that then uses the money to buy that vendor's chips (e.g. NVIDIA's commitments tied to OpenAI; AMD's warrants tied to OpenAI's GPU deployment). Critics warn it can inflate apparent demand.
NVIDIA's May 2023 earnings, when it guided revenue far above expectations (~$11B) and the stock jumped ~24% — the first hard proof in the financials that AI demand was real.
OpenAI's chatbot launched November 30, 2022 and reached ~100M users in two months — the consumer moment that turned AI into a global demand shock the whole chain now serves.
A $500B, four-year AI-infrastructure commitment announced January 2025 by OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle and MGX — the largest single AI build-out plan yet, announced at the White House.
The first big neocloud to go public (March 2025, Nasdaq) — validating the GPU-rental model and its tight ties to NVIDIA, which holds roughly a 12% stake (after a $2B follow-on purchase, Jan 2026).
In July 2025 NVIDIA became the first company ever to reach a $4 trillion valuation — markets treating it as the keystone of the AI economy.
